## Summary

A single AI data center campus proposed for Pike County, Ohio comes with a
dedicated **9.2 gigawatt** natural gas power plant — described by regulators
as capable of "powering more than half of Ohio's typical electrical load."
That's one privately-built power plant, for one computing campus, rivaling
the electricity use of an entire U.S. state.

Numbers like "9.2 GW" are hard to hold in your head. This site tries to make
them tangible by putting them next to something everyone already has an
intuition for: **states**.

## How it works

1. **[Pick one or more data centers](index.qmd)** from a curated list of
   large, publicly-reported U.S. projects.
2. The tool sums their announced power capacity.
3. It then highlights the U.S. states whose combined *average* electricity
   draw adds up to roughly the same amount — using one of two matching
   strategies you can toggle between:
   - **Biggest states first** — accumulate states from largest to smallest
     average power draw until the target is met.
   - **Closest total match** — search for the combination of states whose
     total comes closest to the target.

### Why "average power," not peak demand?

A data center's announced capacity (in MW or GW) is a continuous load — it
runs close to that draw around the clock. To compare fairly, each state's
**annual electricity consumption is converted into an equivalent average
power draw**: `annual GWh ÷ 8,760 hours in a year`. This is the constant
power a state would need if its yearly electricity use were spread evenly
across every hour — directly comparable to a data center's steady-state GW
figure.

As a sanity check: Ohio's 2024 electricity sales imply an average draw of
about **17.6 GW** — consistent with public reporting that the proposed 9.2
GW Pike County plant would represent roughly half of the state's typical
load.

## Data sources

Every dataset used here is documented in full, with retrieval dates and
direct source links, in
[`data/README.md`](https://github.com/jhelvy/datacenter-states/blob/main/data/README.md)
in the project repository. In short:

- **State electricity consumption**: U.S. Energy Information Administration
  (EIA), Form EIA-861 annual retail sales by state (public domain).
- **State boundaries**: U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line shapefiles via the R
  [`tigris`](https://github.com/walkerke/tigris) package, repositioned so
  Alaska and Hawaii appear as insets.
- **Data centers**: hand-curated from public reporting, company
  announcements, and utility/regulatory filings — every project links to
  its source. No free, comprehensive, machine-readable dataset of U.S. data
  center power capacity currently exists; the most complete one we found
  ([Cleanview's behind-the-meter data center report](https://cleanview.co/reports/behind-the-meter-data-centers))
  is paywalled, so this project builds its own small, fully-sourced list
  instead.

## Caveats

- **Announced capacity isn't built capacity.** Figures reflect the best
  public estimates at time of writing and will change as projects are
  built out, delayed, or revised.
- **This is a curated sample, not a census.** The data center list covers
  ~10-15 marquee projects chosen for how well-documented and how large they
  are — it does not attempt to catalog every U.S. data center.
- **Average power, not instantaneous demand.** Real electricity use
  fluctuates hour to hour and season to season for both data centers and
  states; averaging smooths that out in exchange for a fair, simple
  comparison.

## Code

All data processing and cartography run in R; the interactive map is built
with Observable JS and D3. Source: [github.com/jhelvy/datacenter-states](https://github.com/jhelvy/datacenter-states).
